transcript.text: I played Dragon Oath before most people even got their hands on it and I played for early access and I kept coming back
for every major update since. About 60 months ago I made a video asking whether or not you should play it and at the
time Jagex had something promising on their hands, but I was still unsure if the game would make it to release on
time and if my interest for the game would remain. Well, it did and since then a lot has changed. There's new
skills, biomes, bosses and more. So grab a cup of tea and let's go through what's different, what I like about the full
release and ultimately if it's worth your money. You get thrown into the world of Dragon Oath and pretty quickly
realize that you're not at the top of the food chain. Even some of the earlier creatures around the starting area can
give you a little bit of trouble, but it's way way more [music] balanced than the closed beta which was absolutely
brutal. Dragon Oath has a simple straight to the point tutorial quest, but if you venture too far too soon, you
will get punished and I think that's a good thing. Skipping basic dodges or perhaps parries once you have your first
shield will cost you. At the same time the game is tricky enough to a point where you're going to want to pick off
enemies one by one if you can and if your environment allows it and that's something that will continue throughout
the early game. Actually, hold on a second, that's something that you will continue to do throughout the entirety
of the game. You see the world of Ashfall is mostly open world, but that's not to say that you're completely free
to go wherever you want from the start. At the same time it did feel like you had to push into the next biome, avoid
enemies, gather the next tier of war and turn that into a new weapon or piece of equipment before you really had a
fighting chance against the mobs there. And in itself I think that's okay. That's kind of the point of a survival
game. You venture into dangerous areas, take the resources you can get and come back stronger, but that first jump into
bronze felt particularly painful. Anyway, speaking of making things easier, today's sponsor CurseForge is
here to help and if you're playing Dragon Ball Z and want to modify some things, well, with CurseForge app
support, you can browse, install, and manage Dragon Ball Z mods all in one place, and it's free. Simply download
CurseForge from the link below, select RuneScape Dragon Ball Z, and find a mod you like, and hit install. That's it. No
one's more favors. We don't do that here. One thing I'm personally missing in Dragon Ball Z is being able to tank
while moving with magic, and guess what? There's a mod for it, and as you can see, I'm moving around while using magic
attacks. Nice. And for you modders out there, there's $10,000 up for grabs across 23 winners.
So, if you can handle some code and a little suffering if it breaks, check out the Dragon Ball Z modding contest in the
description down below. Make sure you're quick because submissions close on October the 13th.
So, we were just speaking about the struggle of the bronze grind while being able to bump into stronger enemies, or
mainly bosses like the abyssal demon before obtaining bronze gear from Gorn Fells. So, there's this weird situation
in the early game where the game's encouraging you to explore these areas while also making it pretty clear that
you aren't equipped to deal with what was waiting for you there. Also, bosses like the abyssal demon previously could
be cheesed quite easily with safe spots. That's no longer the case in the full release. In fact, it hasn't been the
case for quite some time now as they fixed that early. That's a good thing. We're on the topic of killing things,
and combat is of course part of killing things. Dragon Ball Z combat really doesn't have all that much depth, and
that hasn't really changed for early access, nor with this full release. On paper, there's a lot. We've got
different weapon types, different weapon styles, dodging, blocking, parrying, enchantments, and spells.
The problem is that it doesn't always feel as good as it sounds. In my 100 hours, the majority of the combat was
swiftly attacking enemies to stagger them and overpowering them, or for the larger and chunkier enemies, attacking
from a distance using magic and dodging. Now, that in itself has become far better than what it was before.
Previously, for example, when using magic, you could not cancel your spell. So, if you were in a spell attack animation
and an enemy attacked you, you would get punished again and again. So, combat is
smoother. It has improved. There is more quality of life. It's better in that aspect. But, it still feels fairly flat.
And I say flat because other than your left click attack chain combo and the occasional useful middle mouse button
type, for example, two-handed swords have this spin attack, which is good for AoE, there isn't much more to combat.
You can enchant yourself and make yourself better dodging. You can attack faster by enchanting your weapon with
air or you can apply burns with the enchant with fire spell, which are unlocked after leveling your skills by
fighting things just like regular RuneScape. You gain XP by using melee weapons, for example. There are no
combat abilities that add depth. It's more or less your attack chain plus a bunch of self buffs you activate and
upkeep throughout your combat session. Don't get me wrong, I like what we have, but I feel like there could be more for
this release. I feel like they could have done more with the foundation they've laid for combat. There are some
little things that they've done to make it feel better, of course, like being able to attack while sprinting. That's a
good thing. But, we only really have three types of magic runes, for example. We have air, fire, and water magic.
Where's earth? Where are ancient magics? For how dominant of a combat style magic is, I would have expected there to be
more variation to what I was doing because I pretty much used fire magic for the majority of the early game and
fell hollow with the zombies. And then, I switched to air magic and I stuck there even when I unlocked water magic
or when water magic was added. It's a shame because the animations of water magic are really pretty.
Despite what I said about combat and how it lacked depth, I still found each boss fight to be an enjoyable experience.
Each boss had something unique about it and it felt like a proper boss battle. Some bosses were harder than others, and
I think the boss I struggled the most with was down in reaches boss being the black knight titan. But of course
persistence is key and once you know how to avoid certain attacks, you get the hang of it and it becomes more doable.
Just like Runescape you're rewarded for learning and memorizing mechanics. And what I really liked after killing a boss
is that feeling of unlocking the next biome after an adrenaline filled combat challenge. While I haven't really hunted
any of them so far, I also like that some have replayability in the form of rare drops just like Runescape. There's
also really iconic Runescape items to collect through combat challenges such as the fight caves. Yes, you can unlock
the fire cape in Dragon Ball. Now I have yet to do that and kill Coldra, the final boss of the full release, but it
won't be long before I get there. In fact, the next time I play, I'm going to go for exactly those two things. Now
there are three combat styles in Dragon Ball and you should definitely level them all three for the spells and
passives and enchants, but I found myself relying on melee for any aggressive close proximity monsters and
magic for some good old hit and running from afar. Despite range being fleshed out throughout early access, I don't
think I would use it much with the exception of mini bosses like the Calphite Queen which can throw up
shields to block damage from a certain combat style. The health system is part of combat and has definitely gone
through some changes throughout early access. Originally you had a regular health bar alongside the ward stone aka
shield bar. The problem was that keeping your ward stone topped up became pretty grinding especially when you were
constantly taking damage and having to maintain it. Not very fun. Additionally, as soon as it dropped, you could be one
tapped quite easily. Jagex replaced that system with a straightforward health bar. Now you can increase your maximum
health by finding sanguine urns, but there's no longer that extra shield to constantly maintain. Health potions
surprisingly were also removed which put a lot more emphasis on food and fish for healing and to stain. The system is
better and fits the Runescape theme. The food system has been improved across the board and is more expansive. One thing
that particularly annoyed me in early access was this. Why isn't one piece of food cooked into one piece of cooked
food? Why do I need two to cook food? That's The developers of this game probably had a stroke adding this
because this makes no sense. Why would you try to be different on this level? I don't mind comment made
the difference there, but they changed this. Thank you. One major annoyance of mine in early access was needing to sip
the entire time because thirst drops so so quickly. While it is better, I still feel like I need to drink more than I
would like to, which is something a mod, of course, could fix. But across the board, the food system is significantly
better and instead of munching berries all the time, which is what I did in early access, I now actually actively go
out and make certain food types because they're relevant. Keeping your character
fed is easy in this game as all the food you really need is a good stack of berries. One more thing I want to
mention when it comes to food is fishing because, while it is fairly relevant to get some of the better health regen
foods, it's probably my least favorite skill in the game. And one quest in particular really cemented that for me.
In Umbral Sands, there's a side quest that eventually rewards you with the iconic Obsidian Gate. But right at the
start, you're tasked to get three belt fish along with some cactus steak. And getting those three belt fish made me
want to pull my hair out. Fishing has the stamina mechanic where you have to tire out the fish by moving left and
right using the A and D keys before you can reel it in. And you have to do this multiple times for higher tier fish.
Sounds simple enough, right? Well, apparently the belt fish didn't get the memo. Unless you're doing this little AD
dance perfectly and keeping that tension just right, the fish will be lost. I was desperately trying to catch these fish
like I was trying to diffuse a bomb only for it to escape anyway. Worst of all, I thought I had enough bait every single
time, but because of failed catches and junk, I actually ran out faster than I expected. I actually had to catch six of
these bastards because I had to get three for myself and three for my girlfriend. And after I developed a
genuine hatred for these fish. I wasn't sure if I was playing Dragon Ball Z anymore or participating in a
psychological experiment. Seriously Jagex, where are fishing stamina boosters or drain reducers because as
far as I can tell even with the 1.0 update, that's not really a thing. Or if it is, it's hidden somewhere and I
haven't found it yet. Also, shout-out to my boy Fishing Frenzy for giving me double the catches per successful catch
because without it, I would have genuinely gone insane. Now, those spells are what make Dragon Ball Z feel unique
and honestly, they're one of the biggest reasons progression feels worthwhile. Leveling specific skills like mining
woodcutting and reaching certain thresholds unlock abilities that can genuinely change how you play and gather
resources. And throughout early access, Jagex has added and changed spells. Agility is probably the best example of
a skill that actually changes how you move through the entire world. It was only added later in early access and at
first glance, it might just seem like another skill to level. But the benefits are much more noticeable than that.
Leveling it gets you more mobility, extra carry weight, and important things like double jump and air dashes. And
that can completely change how Ashen Fall feels to navigate. One of the more interesting changes here is Wind Step.
If you played Dragon Ball Z before Agility was introduced, you might remember that Wind Step wasn't locked
behind the skill at all. Well, now it is, but thankfully Agility is kind of fun to train in Dragon Ball Z and it's
kind of strange that I'm saying that because in RuneScape, I think it's one of the worst skills and I'd rather train
it with silverhawk feathers, which actually are in this game, but they're unlocked through doing Agility. Agility
is surprisingly fun in Dragon Ball Z. It's kind of like a parkour mini-game for which you get actual in-game rewards
and you have a personal best timer and depending on that time, you you a reward bag. And if you get gold, you get a good
bag, and you can race your friends, and overall, I think agility is in a nice spot in Runescape Dragon Ball. Ah, [ __ ]
Currently, the 1.0 version Jagex has added a bunch of meat to skills all the way until level 99, including upgrades
to existing skills. Now, you know how we were just talking about wind step? Well, that turns into wind stomp at level 40
agility, which allows you to dive bomb your enemies. I must admit that some skills are pretty
high level, and I'm nowhere close to unlocking all of them, but they add a lot more to the experience and are one
of the strong points of Dragon Ball. [music] Building is also one of the game's unique selling points, and in my
first review video, I said that building was probably what would keep players engaged after they'd finished the main
content. And after spending a lot more time with the game, I still think that's going to be the case. Another thing that
makes the game a lot more enjoyable is being able to traverse the world faster, and Dragon Ball has some mounts you can
unlock, in addition to some skins. First, you unlock a Terrabird and Fell Hollow, and Umbral Sands basically has
its own Uber service, except the Uber is a carpet, and your driver is you. Zooming around the desert with full
freedom, unlike normal Runescape, is quite the treat, I must say. Now, it's not just the mounts. A lot of smaller
quality of life changes, so many I'm not going to cover them in this video, make the game so much better than when I
first started. Think auto sorting. It might not sound particularly exciting, but when you're constantly moving around
and managing your inventory and chests, these are things you can really appreciate. Another thing I'm happy to
say has improved are the raids. A long time ago, in my earlier videos, I complained about being interrupted while
peacefully crafting or gathering by a bunch of goblins deciding it was time to ruin my evening. Thankfully, raids are
now much less frequent and generally feel less disruptive. Another annoyance I mentioned in that video is this. It it
enough, the dragon from the main quest starts launching snot napalm J dams at you every half an hour. It's like a bad
prank. There's no reward. You can't fight back. Folgore doesn't seem to be too interested in dive-bombing me every half
an hour anymore after I took his head. Which is for the best. In my first video, I also said that vaults, which
are Dragon Lords dungeons, felt pretty underwhelming. At least compared to something like Enshrouded. And honestly,
I still think they start off fairly basic and samey, but as you progress through the game, go through the biomes,
the vaults get deeper and more interesting. There's mini bosses, hidden sections, new mechanics, and even light
puzzles. This makes it feel different enough. Not perfect, but different enough. While gear progression isn't all
that different from bronze to runite, it just gets a little bit more grindy and complex materials-wise, each Dragon
Lords biome introduces a mechanic or an environmental hazard, keeping it interesting. I found the soul rifting
mechanic in Fell Hollow to be the most interesting, and I liked that it wasn't just something you had to deal with
while exploring, but that actually had a role in the vaults and the final boss being Amaru, as well. It made the biome
feel more like it had its own identity, rather than just being another area with stronger enemies.
Daudon Reach was probably the prettiest biome, but the least interesting biome mechanically. The whole area had this
magical force preventing you from building, except for a few areas, so you couldn't use loadstones for quick travel
outside the ones you unlocked from the Nexus, which made getting around feel a lot more tedious than it needed to be.
Especially annoying if you ended up dying. That being said, I did like how different the biome felt in terms of
verticality, or being vertical opposed to being horizontal. It also felt like the toughest biome to transition into.
Getting mythril gear felt considerably harder than getting animan in my opinion. And this is where it gets
interesting, because if you asked me why I was playing at different points throughout those 100 hours, I'd probably
give you a different answer each time. 10 hours in, I was trying to see what Dragon Lords was about and if it was was
to hook me. By 30 hours, I was chasing new gear and bosses. And by 60 hours, I'm just building a bit. Every time
Jagex added a new biome, I find myself coming back to see what changed. And 100 hours in, I haven't completed the entire
game. That's partially due to playing in batches alongside updates, but it's also
because the game plays and intrigues you in a way that keeps you curious without
feeling the need to rush the main quest. You might stumble across an NPC, find a hidden cave, or completely sidetrack
yourself chasing a cosmetic or an iconic RuneScape item. There's something strangely peaceful about that, and I
suppose the soundtrack and how the world has been built up has a large role in that. And while I'm not finished, Dragon
Lords isn't finished in every sense of the word, either. There are still things I and others want to see. Think Earth
magic, ancient magics, more combat abilities, and skills like prayer, which are on the road map or horizon.
Also, Jagex, please give me transmogs. If two-piece metal equipment with a major is a matter, then I at least want
to look like a knight using a full three-piece set in addition with a helmet that has a plume. That's all I'm
asking. Also, there's another resource tier coming up, so there's clearly room for Dragon Lords to grow. So, is Dragon
Lords worth it? At 30 euros, I think there's a pretty compelling amount of survival game here. If you're a
RuneScape fan, there's obviously a lot that will feel familiar, but you don't need to know RuneScape to enjoy Dragon
Lords. If you're coming from games like Valheim or Enshrouded, which I've both played, I think Dragon Lords has enough
of its own identity now that it's more than just a survival game wearing a RuneScape skin.
It isn't perfect. The combat could be deeper, some progression can still feel rough, and there are systems I'd like to
see expanded. But that's a very different conclusion from one when I had first played it. Back then, I saw a
promising survival game that wasn't quite finished. After 100 hours and a 1.0 update, I still think it isn't
finished, but it's a worthy survival game part of the RuneScape franchise. Dragon Lords never needed to be the
perfect survival game, but for a game this young, it does a fantastic job of being a survival game while still
retaining enough of that RuneScape identity to feel unique and appealing to a much wider audience. And after 100
hours, I can confidently say Jagex delivered. Thank you for watching. And a thank you to CurseForge for sponsoring
this video.

to me the game feels far from done. the tier progression leaves a lot to be desired. it doesn't make sense that vestige items are just reskins of the same ore tier, all set bonuses are the same. plus there doesn't seem to be enough enemy variety across the zones especially in the kuldra raid and dungeons. there's just so much missed potential with unique gear, set bonuses, and special attacks. nothing gives you that feeling of being "overpowered" while it still being relevant. it always feels as if no matter what "masterwork" weapon or armor you have, you're still struggling against 2-3 mobs of the same tier. and by the time you actually craft your vestiges you're already moving on to the next area which instantly makes your set obsolete. I don't know man... i really want to like it. i beat the game and sunk over 70 hours into it. but something has always felt missing throughout the playthrough.
